The interest on the .investment would not exceed $3,600, so that you have quite a margin.
But you still have to pay fuel and light.
The Minister of Militia says he was in error in saying $6,400 ; he now says it is only $4,440. They had better arrage between them as to which is correct.

While I quite agree that the government and parliament should be prudent in expenditure, I deny that the state of the money market could be any ground for the government delaying its obligations where the construction of public buildings has been entered on. I also deny that it is a time when the government' should refuse to go on with the construction of public works which are in the interest of the people of this country. Except that the interest rafe is higher now than it was formerly, I deny that money cannot be obtained by the issue of ordinary securities. Only a short time ago the Pennsylvania Railway Company asked for a $40,000,000 loan on their debentures and .they received offers for $1,000,000,000. The rate of interest is higher than it was a couple of years ago because there are other classes of securities than government securities which investors are beginning to regard as safe, but outside of the interest I do not think there ever was a better time to obtain money than at present. The interest is reasonably high for permanent loans. The Pennsylvania loan was 4 per cent.

I draw the attention of the minister to the fact that a vote of $6,000 was taken for these buildings in 1906. The hon. minister has made the price very high. I will read what the Minister of Public Works at that time, Mr. Hyman, stated :
This is not commenced. The Militia and Defence Department desire to build quarters for the married non-commissioned officers of A squadron of the permanent force, which will cost in the neighbourhood of $40,000; a guard room, prisoners' room, lecture room, &c., at a cost of $22,000; and a stores building at a cost of $4,000, making a total of $66,000. These will be built on government property.
Now, my hon. friend states that these will cost upwards of $90,000.
The minister was within the mark, so far as the cost of the building is concerned. The addition is for furnishings and fittings.
What is a guard room for?	*
The chief purpose of a guard room is to confine men temporarily who have been disobedient or have violated the rules.

You build a guard room 82 feet by 31 feet for a squad of 100 men, more or less. The cost of the building, without anything else is $25,000, to furnish a place where you may keep safely an occasional disorderly soldier.

Besides the guard room, there are to be temporary offices, a prisoners' room, district officer's offices, and orderly room, a clerks' room and a store room. This new building was recommended by the district officer commanding.
There is no reason why all that could not be provided for $10,000.
May I ask the date of that report of Colonel Evans?

This is simply a memorandum prepared for me by the deputy minister, and it has no date. It was prepared during the present session, but I fancy that this communication was over a year ago, before the first estimates were brought down.
Mr. PERLEY- I would like again to refer to the item on page Y-63 of the Auditor General's Report-' Winnipeg military buildings: quarters for non-commissioned officers, including guard rooms, &c., J. & J. McDiarmid Company, contract for building complete, $2,600.' The minister said this must be a mistake, but it cannot be, because the item is carried over to the total on page V-4.

It is clearly a mistake. That would be simply a payment made on account, because the amount of the contract of McDiarmid & Company is $25,475.
Brandon drill hall, $20,000.

I promised to give the hon. member for Leeds and Grenville the total amount of the progress estimates to date. They amount to $37,637, less 10 per cent drawback, $3,763, leaving a balance of $33,874, of which $23,010 has been paid to date, leaving a balance due of $10,864.
How large is the site ?
215 feet by 110 feet.
What did it cost?
Barracks for permanent corps-Strathcona Horse, $40,000.
It is intended to erect a barracks for the Strathcona Horse ? This is a revote.
Where is it located ?
It is not located.

It has been in the estimate for 3 or 4 years. The idea was to preserve the name and perpetuate the fame of the Strathcona Horse, a very desirable object in which the whole House agreed on every occasion when I brought the matter up. The difficulty has been to locate the Strathcona Horse, and I must confess I have not been able to do so yet. I believe it has now come down to a choice between Calgary and Medicine Hat. A report was made by a military board some years ago as to the proper place, from a military stanpoint, for the location of this force with a view to its utilization for purposes of traiuing. As the committee knows, the chief business of the permanent force is to educate the officers and non-commissioned officers in the active militia. The desire is to have the corps conveniently situated so that advantage can be taken of it by the active militia throughout the new provinces. I hope that in the next few weeks the question will be determined.
What does the board say ?
The board says either Calgary or Medicine Hat. From a military point of view hither would accommodate the active militia and strategically either place would be equally good.
Have you a permanent force called the Strathcona Horse ?

Only the nucleus. WTe have created a new military district and placed it under the command of Colonel Steele, who is quartered at Calgary at present with a small staff. He is doing good work there and is eminently qualified to do the work required there. He was the commanding officer of the Strathcona Horse, as the committee will remember. Lord Strathcona was consulted about this very matter and as to the officers. We thought it right to pay him the compliment, as the corps was named after him and in view of all he had done in connection with it, of asking him for his views with regard to it, and while he did not insist on anything he was very much pleased indeed to think we were going to select as many as possible of the officers who served with the corps in South Africa.
Are they to be mounted rifles ?
Yes, they are to be mounted rifles.

In connection with the selection of the site I wish to put it on. record that in my opinion there can be nodebate or hesitation as to the choice between Calgary and Medicine Hat. The first essential is that the site should be central. . The minister has explained that this is for the use of the three great prairie provinces and we all know that Calgary is on the extreme western frontier. As between Medicine Hat and Calgary there can be no doubt that Medicine Hat is the more central. More than that, Medicine Hat has in view a very suitable location across the Saskatchewan river and within a few mouths there will be opened for traffic a bridge across the river at this point. While no suitable grounds are in view at Calgary, I submit there is a much stronger case in favour of Medicine Hat.

It might be a question which is the most central point for the corps likely to be raised in that country. Calgary would be most suitable for the corps situated north of Calgary. Perhaps the minister could say where the corps likely to send officers and non-commissioned officers for instruction are chiefly situated. Where are the headquarters of those at present in Alberta ?

In the two provinces there are the Alberta Rangers, regimental headquarters, McLeod ; Saskatchewan Light Horse, A squadron, Saskatchewan, B, Lloydminster ; Independent squadrons; Alberta Mounted Rifles, regimental headquarters Edmonton ; A and D siquadrons, Edmonton, B, Strathcona, C, Fort Saskatchewan ; 16th Mounted Rifles regimental headquarters, Regina, A squadron, Moosomin, B, Moosejaw, C, Regina, D, Grenfell ; 15th Light Horse, regimental headquarters, Calgary, A and D squadrons, Calgary, B, Cochrane, C, High River.

At present there is no mounted corps at Medicine Hat. The minister ought certainly to consider the convenience of the corps at present organized in that country and those likely to be organized in the future. The minister, I presume, must also consider the advantage of having the headquarters in a large centre where it is a good thing to' foster the military spirit. I hope the minister will take all these matters into consideration and will weigh the merits of either place before he comes to a decision.

I am glad to have the views otf my hon. friend and of all the hon. members who represent the

western provinces. In justice to Medicine Hat, I should say that I overlooked one corps, Independent Squadron D, headquarters at Medicine Hat.

I would point out that over half of the corps whose names have been read out by the minister are at present more convenient to Medicine Hat than to Calgary. Moreover, the bulk 'of the future population of those provinces will be more convenient to Medicine Hat than to Calgary. It does not make much difference as to distance, because in either case the militia would have to take the train to go there. It is only a matter of a few miles difference. But so far as the centre of the bulk of the population is concerned Medicine Hat is rather more so than Calgary.
Will this be for the benefit of the three provinces ?
We have a cavalry school at Winnipeg now.
You have no infantry in Alberta and Saskatchewan ?
I think there is one regiment being organized in Alberta at or near Edmonton, and there is a regiment in Manitoba.

I agree with the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) that it does not make much difference which place you choose, as the matter of distance would be about equal. But you ought to have an attractive place where the officers and noncommissioned officers will be tempted to go.
When may we expect that a decision will be come to with reference to the location ?

I have been waiting for advice and assistance in this matter, it may be settled at any moment. So far as I am concerned, I have an open mind. I hope it will be settled during the present year. I may say with regard to the active militia to be accommodated, that portions of British Columbia have to be considered as well as these two new provinces, because no doubt the school, where-ever it is established, will be utilized to some extent by the militia of the eastern part of British Columbia.
Mr. IfOWLER. What quantity of land is it proposed to acquire ?

I believe there is no difficulty whatever about the land, whether we locate at Calgary or at Medicine Hat. There is a large quantity of land in both places owned by the Northwest Mounted Police, and which is available.

When you say a large quantity, how much do you mean ?
348*

We ought
to have fifty acres or a hundred acres, fifty would do pretty well.
I think two hundred would be even better, because it would be used as a drill ground and for tactical movements. You cannot have too much.
I do not remember the exact amount, but I am told there is plenty of land available at either of these places.
As the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. McCarthy) is not here, I think this item ought to stand. We want to get some information from him as to what is likely to be the total cost of this land.

Let the item be carried now, and we will give him a chance of discussing it later on.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, before we proceed with the discussion of the items of Supply, there is another matter which I wish to mention, and I will do it in a moment while a quorum is gathering-there is not a quorum here at present. I am glad to see the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) in his place. I would ask him if, when he came into this Chamber from the corridor, he did not notice how, in contrast with the air there, the air in the Chamber was foul? I believe a large amount of money was spent a few years ago to try to improve the ventilation of this room. But, in my opinion, the steps then taken were not so effectual as would be the mere opening of these upper windows to admit fresh air and let the foul air escape. The air here is something awful, as you come out of the corridor. I mentioned it to two or three members and they feel about it as I do. I would urge the minister to give instructions to have the windows opened, and let us have fresh air from outside.

I have spoken to the chief architect with regard to the ventilation, and he says that the opening of the upper windows would interfere with the circulation of air which comes in from below, and make the situation worse than it is.
The same statement was made two or three years ago, but some of us insisted that the windows should be opened and after it was done, all agreed that it was a great improvement.

The chief architect tells me that he cannot make the change to-

night, but he will try on Monday and see If it does good.

I would ask the Minister of Public Works to consider the idea of a roof-garden in connection with this House, or a pavilion on the lawn. If we are to have summer sessions, we could be much more comfortable in a pavilion.
Would the hon. gentleman (Mr. W. F. Maclean) suggest that we should hold our session in the roof garden?
Certainly. Some kind of canopy or awning could be provided making an ideal chamber in weather of this kind, particularly as compared with this.

McCarthy. Mr. Chairman, before six o'clock, the item under discussion was the vote for the barracks for the Strathcona Horse. This item is not a new one. There has been an item in the estimates for this purpose ever since I have been in this House, and I do not know how many years before. I understand that the only thing preventing the building of the barracks, which is greatly needed, is that certain representations have been made to the Minister of Militia as to the point at which the barracks should be built. I have repeatedly made representations both in this House and out of it to the Minister of Militia and the officers of the Militia Department regarding the suitability of the city of Calgary for such purpose. I do not propose to take up the time of the House repeating in detail what those representations were, for the simple reason that some three years ago the Minister of Militia and a number of his officers went through the western country for the purpose of satisfying themselves where this barracks should be established. There can be absolutely no doubt in the mind of any man as to the proper place for the barracks, and that proper place is the city of Calgary.
Mr, GRAHAM. Hear, hear.

McCarthy. I am glad to find that I have one of the members of the government, the Minister of Railways and Canals, to agree with me in this matter. The officers of the department are quite able to satisfy their own minds as to this point. Though the matter was investigated some three years ago, for some reason the construction of the building has been delayed-what the reason may be I do not know. There are many reasons which combine to make the city of Calgary a most desirable point. In the first place, it is the best place for recruiting men; it is centrally located to recruit men from Alberta, British Columbia and the western part of Saskatchewan. It is also the best place for recruiting horses. There is more interest taken in military matters In the Mr. PUGSLEY.
city of Calgary than in any other place in the middle west. The city of Calgary is the largest city between Winnipeg and Vancouver. From what I could gather from the representations made here this afternoon, it was suggested by the members for East and West Assiniboia that Calgary might be an inconvenient point for young men from Saskatchewan who wanted to recruit. But, Mr. Chairman, they have a barracks in Winnipeg, and if you look at the map you will see that Winnipeg would be more desirable to the eastern part of Saskatchewan than Medicine Hat would be-against which latter place I have nothing to say-but, naturally, these men would go to the city of Winnipeg rather than to Medicine Hat because, as I understand it, that section is in the Winnipeg military district at the present time. Further consulting the map, the minister will see that young men who desire to attend the barracks from north of Calgary-from Edmonton and all the places south of Edmonton-if required to go to Medicine Hat, would have to pass through the city of Calgary to reach their destination. The reason Edmonton was chosen as the capital of the province of Alberta, I understand, was that it was said to be the centre of the province by the Prime Minister. Now, Calgary is 190 miles south of Edmonton. So, the men from the alleged central part of Alberta would have to pass through Calgary and go 380 miles east to Medicine Hat; the same argument applies in the case of those coming from British Columbia. I have already said that there is no place in the west that has taken a greater interest in matters military than the city of Calgary. For some years a number of the citizens there kept up a drili hall at their own expense. According to the Dominion census of 1896, not only is Calgary the largest city between Winnipeg and Vancouver, but without its suburbs it has a population 9,000 greater than that of Medicine Hat. For all these reasons, I submit there can be no good ground for taking away this barracks, which, it is generally understood, was to be established at Calgary. Colonel Steele is there and camp is now being held at Calgary. It was held there last year because it was the most convenient place and the place where all the men who take an interest in military matters prefer to go to attend camp. I hope the minister will see to it that justice is done. Though Calgary is the largest city between Winnipeg and Vancouver, practically no public money has been spent there since 1896 by the Laurier administration, except for some improvements on the post office. I warn the minister not to continue that policy of discrimination as it cuts both ways, but to deal with the city of Calgary justly and fairly. I have no doubt as to the determination he will come to if re will consult

with the officers of the Militia Department who visited that country three years ago.

I need only say that the location of this barracks will, of course, rest with my colleague the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden). He is not present at this moment, but I feel sure that I can say for him that he will weigh most carefully the respective advantages of Calgary and Medicine Hat and will arrive at such a decision as he believes in the public interest.
Public Works, chargeable to income-rents, repairs, furniture, heating, &c.-'Ottawa public buildings including repairs, ventilation, lighting, furniture, &c., $175,000.

This vote is for the purpose of carrying on the improvements and repairs and the purchase of furniture, fittings and other supplies which are found to be necessary from time to time to maintain the public buildings in the city of Ottawa in a proper state of efficiency to meet the requirements of the public service. These works are mainly performed by the mechanics and labourers of the Department of Public Works and are under the direct supervision of the officers of that department. The amount is exactly the same as that voted last year.
Was it all expended ?
X think it was all expended.
Perhaps the minister would specify how much of this was for ventilation, how much for lighting and how much for furniture.

It is impossible to give my hon. friend that information. It is estimated that for wages there will be required $96,141.10 ; staff, mechanics and engineers, about $29,910 ; purchase of materials, $48,948.90, making the total required $175,000.
Rents, Dominion public buildings, $133,000.
This is to pay the rent of buildings occupied by the government in the city of Ottawa and throughout the Dominion. The appropriation last year was the same.
What amount is paid in Ottawa ?
How much in Toronto ?
I should think about. $7,000.
Have you rented any other buildings in Ottawa since last year ?

We have rented the other half of the Canadian building, the
Seybold building for customs purposes and a portion of the Trafalgar building for the Department of the Interior. Since I have been minister I have been pressed very much by different departments to give them additional accommodation, among others the Department of the Interior, the penitentiary branch, the Department of Customs and I have endeavoured to meet their requirements. As hon. gentlemen are aware parliament has approved of the erection of an additional departmental building, but the construction has not yet commenced and in the meantime we .are obliged to rent accommodation.
Is any headway being made with the new building ?

Nothing beyond acquiring the property. We have put in the estimates $250,000 and it is not impossible that during recess we may take action towards the erection of a building, but as to that,
1 cannot say.
You will not have time ; the elections will be on.

Are they coming on ?
I thank my hon. friend for the information.
How much is being paid for the Seybold building ?
Who does the repairing ? Mr. PUGSLEY. The department.
What is the estimated cost of these repairs ?

The work is being done by the staff of the department and I suppose the cost will run up to perhaps $5,000.
Mr.-FOWLER. What happens to the rents of those properties on Mackenzie avenue which have been acquired by the government ?
The rents are being collected by the department.
What income did the department receive from rents last year 1
About $6,000. Some of the buildings have been pulled down.
Do you rent the church ?
We are not getting a rental from the church.
I should hope not.

There are some few private owners who asked what we thought was a higher price than the government ought to pay for their properties. The department took the necessary steps to expropriate and then the payments filed in the ordinary way, their petitions of right to be paid compensation to be determined by the Exchequer court.

How much do you pay for the other half of the Canadian building ?
Mr. PUGSIjEY. The total amount is $12,539.60. For the additional half we pay $15,209.60.
That is a large rent for one building.
It is only 41 cents per superficial foot which is regarded as a low rental in Ottawa.
What is the extent of the property that the government purchased for the new building which they intend erecting?
It is a very large area, taking in the church on Sussex street and Mackenzie avenue and extending down to the Mint.
Does it take the Lindsay building?

No. The purchase of the Lindsay building is under consideration, but it would cost pretty nearly as much as all the rest of the property, and we did not think it was necessary to have it, or that we would be justified in paying a large sum for it.
Has the staff of the Customs Department been so much increased in the past year that it is necessary to get accommodation in the Seybold block?
That is for the Ottawa Custom-house, outside service. It formerly was near the Rideau Club, and we have removed it and put the Penitentiary branch in its place.
Is the Penitentiary branch so large that you require a separate building outside of the East Block?
We have had constant and pressing demands from the Justice Department for further accommodation.
There seems to bfc great extravagance and waste in connection with these things.
The accommodation in the East Block is very limited as compared with the number of occupants.
Some of the offices in the Auditor General's Department are very small ; are you giving him more room?
We have given the Auditor General's Department some rooms In the Canadian building.

It is very inconvenient to separate these branches of different departments and give them offices Mr. BLAIN.
in different parts of the city. They should be kept together as much as possible.
I agree with that, and we have endeavoured to arrange it with that end in view.
Would it not be better to remove one entire department to another building rather than to separate branches of the same department?
The heads of the de partments prefer the arrangement we have made.

Has the Minister of Public Works ever directed his attention to the erection of modern administrative buildings similar, for example, to' the Traders' Bank building in Toronto, which occupies a comparatively small lot of land, but in which 1,500 people can be accommodated? There is a new kind of architecture that they call the administrative building, which, at comparatively small cost, gives abundance of light and space. There is no striving for architectural effect, but the architects strive to apply modern experience to the office accommodation which the building should afford. It is high time for our Department of Public Works to abandon the old idea of architectural effect and come nearer to the modern idea. In Washington they are coming to adopt this style of building, and it is well worthy the consideration of the government here. I would like to see an experiment made with an administrative building of that kind in the city of Ottawa.
Twenty-two stories ?
Yes, if you like ; the new municipal building in New York is to be thirty stories.

In the construction of the new post office at Montreal we are not paying so much attention to architectural effect as to affording ample light and space and accommodation. I doubt very much if the public would approve of erecting these huge sky scrapers in the capital city of Ottawa, where the laud is somewhat abundant and where the general desire seems to be to have ample ground in connection with all buildings. I think it would be a mistake to erect these very high buildings in Ottawa.

I am not advocating sky scrapers, but I am advocating buildings of several stories, which would give plenty of space and light. If you had a six-story building here you would marvel at the accommodation you would get.

I cannot agree with my hon. friend from South York with regard to public buildings. While attention should be paid to utility in erecting these public buildings, attention should also be paid to

architectural beauty as well. There Is no reason why these buildings should not be architecturally beautiful as well as in the highest sense useful. With regard to providing office room for the public service, that is a matter the government seems to have neglected very much, and it should be taken up at once. It does not seem to me to be right that the civil service should be scattered ail over the city in .buildings in most cases entirely unsuitable for the purpose, and the government should enter on a large scheme of providing suitable office buildings. It is not well for the service that too many clerks should be congregated together in one room. They certainly cannot and do not perform their duties as well as they would if they were separated more. They get talking together about the last tennis game when they should be attending to their public duties. I believe you could do with fewer public servants if they were provided with proper offices.

I am quite in accord with the idea the hon. member has just expressed, and the government, recognizing it, has engaged to construct new departmental *buildings with a view to properly housing the public officials ; but we are obliged to rent these buildings temporarily until the new-buildings are completed. It must be home in mind that in addition to the cost of the land, which is considerable, these buildings, which are to include accommodation for the various departments now needing it and also a palace of justice for the Supreme Court, will cost a very large sum- in the vicinity of $4,000,000. Considering the financial condition which came upon this country as well as upon other countries of the world last fall, we thought it was not desirable then to enter upon the work of building. We thought we might acquire the land and get our title completed, and during this season complete the plans and specifications as well as call for tenders for the work, but not engage vigorously in the work of construction perhaps until next year. A vote of $250,000 for the work has already been passed, and it is not unlikely that we may take the necessary steps to complete the plans and specifications and call for tenders for the work.
Has the minister a lease of the Seybold block ?
Yes, a lease for five years.
Are there taxes upon the property, and if so, what are they ?
We pay the taxes. They are $2,000.
That makes a little over $8,000, besides $5,000 for fitting up.
Yes, but that expenditure would be for the five years, and we have the right of renewal.
What is the value of the property ?
It is a five story building. I suppose the building and land would be worth $60,000 or $70,000, perhaps $100,000.
Is it the intention to occupy all the five stories ?

We have the five stories available if we need them all, but at present we allow the Customs Department to occupy two floors. With regard to taxes,
I may say that an Act of the Ontario legislature provides for the taxation of buildings which are rented by the government.
I would not be disposed myself to raise any question with regard to that, because it seems to me that it would be a great hardship on the city of Ottawa that a private building that would pay taxes if rented by a private individual would escape taxation when rented to the government. My own view would be that, unless there was something exceptional in the law, the property would be taxable, because the assessment would be against the owner, and I do not see why he should escape taxation simply because the property is occupied by the Crown. The owner will just add the amount of the taxes to the rental.
What amount of public improvements were made on the Seybold building ?

The improvements will be made by the men regularly employed by the department. I am not able to state exactly what they will cost, but probably in the vicinity of $5,000, for altering the partitions and putting in counters and fittings.
And an elevator ?
There is an elevator in the building, put in by the owner.

Those who are on the monthly list are allowed two weeks each year, and they may select their own time, provided their services are not urgently required, and if they are off for a day or two, the time is counted against their two weeks.

I put another question as follows :
1.	Is Mr. Arthur Caron in the employ of the Department of Public Works as a subordinate to M. Paul Reinhardt ? If so, what was he employed at on the 8th of June, 1908?
2.	Is Octave Thiberge also in same employ? If so, what was he employed at on the same day?

speakeroldname: Hon. WM. PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
Arthur Caron and Hubert Theberge (not Octave Thiberge) are employed under Mr. Reinhardt, on the carpenters' staff of the Public Works Department. Neither of these men reported for duty on June 8.
I want to read to the hon. minister some correspondence which I have received in reference to these gentlemen :
Dear Mr. Taylor,-You may interest a lot of local people, particularly in Hull, by putting a question in the House in order to find out why it is that ever since 1896, one Paul Reinhardt, a French Canadian of Hull, who is superintendent of the Public Works Department's shop on Wellington street, Ottawa. has been allowed to take the government time to meddle actively and offensively in every election, municipal, provincial and federal, in favour of Grit candidates? He was appointed by the Liberals in 1896. Moreover, he brings his squad of subordinates from the shops and places them in the polls to represent his candidates. That is what he is doing again in Hull to-day, and it is and has been a scandal for Hull for twelve years now. You had better have an inquiry made also of how it came about that his brother's house in Hull was partly built by the shop's staff and with the shop's stuff.
This is followed by another letter:
Hull, June 10, 1908.
Dear Mr. Taylor,-Following my first letter,
I must not say that the man Reinhardt was head canvasser for Gendron. His subordinate at the government shop, Mr. Arthur Caron, was deputy returning officer in a poll on Victoria ^ street in Hull. The Hull men on his staff in Ottawa and who partook in the election are Octave Theberge, and a half dozen others. Now this has been going on, I say, for twelve years at every election, mind you every election, municipal, provincial and federal.
Yours truly.
He then wrote :
Hull, June 12, 1908.
Dear Mr. Taylor,-All of that Hull crew of Reinhardt worked in Hull all the week previous to the election, that is from first to eighth of June. Moreover, one Remillard, and one, Thomas Caron, of Hull, two elevator men in the Post Office Department, took the week Mr TAYLOR.
here for the same purpose. You want to look out whether they'll be paid for that.
All Reinhardt's staff, six from Hull, worked here for eight days.
The last letter reads :
Hull, June 15, 1908.
Dear Mr. Taylor,-It appears that this Reinhardt affair is a preconcerted scheme. They have right to holidays and are paid for it. So they all took their holidays at once, they will get paid for it and they came to work here eight days earning the money that other political workers would have been glad to earn.
You might also inquire what became of Mr. Tarte s boat-house, worth $400, which used to be anchored at government $50,000 dock here, whether one Tom Caldwell borrowed it and is nowhere to be found, or who bought it and how much was paid for it. Also who is allowed to store boats, launches, &c., in that dock.
There is a state of affairs that is true and I think it my duty to bring it to the attention of the minister.
By whom is it signed ? Mr. TAYLOR. It is not signed.

Mr. Chairman, I would ask my hon. friend whether he thinks it fair that he, as a member of parliament, having no knowledge of the truth of these matters himself, should read in parliament an anonymous letter, a letter to which the writer is ashamed or afraid to put his signature, and have these charges against employees of the department spread upon the record.

I give this as information coming to me, apd I believe from the minister's answers to the questions I asked that these statements are true. Reinhardt was there for a week and the minister said he was on his holidays. The other man was deputy returning officer, an employee paid by the government and he was, allowed to go there and take part in thei election. If this is so, the minister should dismiss the whole staff. I believe the information is correct.
What knowledge have you that warrants you in believing it is true ?
I have some knowledge outside of that. The gentleman told me he would send the facts, I know the party who sent it.
What is his name ?

That is a private matter.
I want to give the information and let the minister investigate it because I do not think the country has a right to pay these men for holidays when they are taking part in elections This man is a civil servant drawing $85 a month and he should not be taking part in elections. Reinhardt was the head pusher for Gendron' and one of

the others was deputy returning officer. It is the minister's duty to parliament and to the country to investigate and if these statements are true dismiss the men, one and all.

I think it is the duty of the man who gave the information to my hon. friend if he knows, as he states, that the house of a brother of Reinhardt has been built by the Public "Works staff out of material belonging to the Public Works Department, to go before a magistrate and lay an information.
I shall give the minister the gentleman's name privately.

That was the man's duty and it was the duty of my horn friend instead of reading the letter in parliament, to have so advised him. When my hon. friend asked the questions the other day I made inquiry and I was informed that so far from its being true that this man's brother had built a house with the labour of members of the Public Works staff and with material from the Public Works Department-
Partly.

-his brother had not built a house at all. As far as going on holidays is concerned, Reinhardt is foreman of the department and is entitled to two weeks holidays the same as other foremen and superintendents. The time he was away will be charged against his holidays. With regard to the other man, who did not report for duty, it often happens that men employed by the day do not report for duty. The direction I have given is that they shall be docked their pay on the days they are away and these men who were employed by the day and absent on the occasion of which my hon. friend speaks will not be paid by the department for that time.

Does the minister think it quite proper, keeping in view the policy of the government, that this gentleman, an employee of the government, should act as deputy returning officer in the recent elections ? '
I see no objection to a man occupying the position of deputy returning officer, it is a non-partisan position.
My hon. friend surely has forgotten the resolution that was passed by this House unanimously in respect of employees taking an active part in political elections.
But a deputy returning officer is not supposed to take any part and must not.
My hon. friend would not venture to state that before the House and ask us to accept it seriously ?
I certainly would.
Every one knows that when a man is appointed deputy returning officer he is a supporter of the government, he is an active politician.
Am I to understand that my hon. friend is confessing that in the recent elections in Ontario the deputy returning officers were partisans and took part in the elections ? That is a new doctrine.
In the last election in New Brunswick Conservative after Conservative was appointed. I am surprised the hon. gentleman will confess what his friends were doing in Ontario.
I never thought my hon. friend would venture to mention New Brunswick again.
You amaze me by the statement that the deputy returning officer is a partisan.
I am surprised to hear my hon. friend make the confession he made here.

My friend is not at all so innocent as he would like the House to believe. Neither is the minister himself. He is a politician and knows something about politics in his own province. He has taken an active part. Every member of this House knows that while we have party government here, in the main It is friends of the government who are appointed deputy returning officers in every election. How the minister would venture to support a government whose policy it is that no official shall take an active part in the elections and then defend this man acting in this way during his vacation

In the province from which I come I do not believe there is a single sheriff who would appoint as deputy a man who had taken an active part in the election. They are always careful to get men in whom both sides will have confidence, men who did not take an active part in the elections.

The hon. gentleman travels entirely outside the lines of the policy of the government of which he is a member when he says that an employee of the government receiving a pretty large salary has the right to take part in a provincial election, such an active part as to be a deputy returning officer.
The man was a day labourer, and was not paid for the day he was absent.

That is not the point. The people of this country will not understand that the government is carrying out its declared policy when a member of the cabinet will justify a government employee taking a part in a provincial election, so active a part-I repeat-as to be a deputy returning officer.
Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) tell the committee what active part a deputy returning officer takes in an election?

The hon. gentleman is not so clever as he may think. The hon. gentleman himself is a politician of the partisan kind, or he would not occupy his present position. I do not find fault with party politics; I believe in it and the people of this country believe in it.' There is no use in the hon. gentleman pretending that a deputy returning officer is not a partisan; everybody knows he is. Yet the minister justifies a civil servant in taking an active part in politics and accepting the position of deputy returning officer. The people of this country will note with interest what the minister has said, in contrast with the declaration of the Prime Minister that, while civil servants have the right to vote, they shall not take an active part in an election.

As I have stated, the man who acted as deputy returning officer, as the hon. gentleman says, was employed by the day; he could come to-day and stay away to-morrow. On the day he did not report for duty he was not paid by the department. I am not prepared to say that there is any objection in an employee of the government, a day labourer, on the day when he is not under pay of the department, acting as a deputy returning officer. The hon. gentleman puts it that I have countenanced employees of the department taking an active part in politics and acting as deputy returning officers. I said nothing of that kind. I declared with the utmost sincerity that I did not look upon the position of deputy returning officer as that of a partisan. I do not think he ought to show any interest in an election one way or the other. And, if the sheriff does his duty, he will not appoint any man as deputy returning officer except one who, he believes, will be impartial as between the parties. My hon. friend (Mr. Blain) must have had an experience different from that of those of us who come from a different part of the Dominion. I am surprised to hear that in the province of Ontario the position of deputy returning officer is regarded-as, judging from his statements, it appears to be-as a partisan position and one which is properly filled by a partisan. I am surprised to hear him say that the man who takes the position as a deputy returning officer is assumed, from Mr. PUGSLEY.
that very fact, to be taking an active part in politics. The only way he could take an active part would be by seeking in some way by his action on the day of election to secure the return of the candidate of the party who had chosen him for the position. I do not believe that the premier of Ontario would subscribe to the doctrine which the hon. gentleman puts forward. I do not look upon the position of deputy returning officer as a partisan position. He is like a judge; he is supposed to be impartial
He takes an oath to be impartial.
Yes, and he violates his oath of office if he acts in any except the most impartial manner.

The returning officers in Ontario are the sheriffs and registrars, most of whom have been appointed by the Liberal party. These men might be accused of partisanship just as much as the deputy returning officer. I have never heard any complaint made against the appointment of sheriffs and registrars to the position of returning officers, and I see no reason why there should be any objection against deputy returning officers being appointed from the ranks of public officers.

Just to show what partisanship does in the province of Ontario, I may say that this government appointed a returning officer in my county. I asked to get rid of this man Hawkeye and he refused. And this was the man who afterwards handled the bogus ballots and had the trick ballot box. The government has done nothing to stop him. He is running about the country and has been here in this city. I think the government should look after such men.

I wish simply to bring the question back to where we started from. I heard the Prime Minister of this country, within the last month, say in this House that he was a partisan. Does the Minister of Public Works wish to imply that Sir Wilfrid Laurier would not be a fit man to make a deputy returning officer ? He fails to draw the distinction between a partisan and an offensive partisan. Now, coming back to the question before the committee of buildings rented for the Department of Justice, I find, under the head of Civil Government last year, there were twenty-two employees in the Justice Department, and there are the same number this year. Now I am at a loss to- understand, if twenty-two officials of the department found accommodation in the eastern block last year, how it comes that these same offices are not fit to accommodate the same number of men this year ?
They were cramped for space.
They do not appear to have been cramped last year.
Yes, they were.
Have they grown a little more corpulent under this grafting government ?
Order.
Who. is out of order?
The hon. gentleman.
Has it come to be out of order to call this government a grafting government ?
It is clearly out of order.
WTell, I am sorry to see that the hon. gentleman has not a very proper conception of the meaning of the English language.

I think the hon. gentleman should withdraw that expression. I think there is nothing more disorderly than to make a statement of that kind. Sup-

pose an hon. member on this side of the House were to make a charge of that kind against members of the opposition who had been members of a government, he would be clearly out of order. You can not make a charge against members of this House who happen to be members of the government collectively, which you would not be permitted to make against an individual member of the House.
Yes, you can.

I am sorry the minister has become so extremely sensitive. I think perhaps before this session closes he will have opportunities for curbing his sensitiveness if he is going to get riled or feel offended at such a reference. I did not intend to make it in an offensive way. 1 think it has ceased to be an offensive expression to say that a man is a grafter. It is an expression so well understood in connection with this government nobody thinks there is anything wrong about it.
I rise to a point of order. What does grafter mean ?
Now I do not propose to be schoolmaster for the hon. gentleman.
I would like very well to have a definition of grafter.
Has the hon. gentleman been grafting, too, that he becomes so sensitive ?
I have been charged by my late political opponent with graft to the extent of $31,000, and four questions were placed on the Order Paper for my particular benefit regarding the charge.

That is news to me. I thought the hon. gentleman was too old a member of parliament to get frightened at the idea of grafting. I am not imputing anything to him. When I made use of the term I did not make use of it in any offensive way. That word has become so common that I would not think any member of this House would feel hurt if the term was directed to himself. Now, we will get back to the Department of Justice.
I hope the hon. gentleman will discuss it in a gentlemanly manner.
Does the minister mean to insinuate that I have been ungentlemanly?

I do, decidedly. In my judgment, in an assembly of gentlemen, it is not proper to apply to any member of this House, or to any six members of this House, the expression which the hon. gentleman has used. I do not think it is in order, and on reflection the hon. gentleman will see that an expression of that kind will not add to the dignity of discussion in the Mr. PUGSLEY.
House. I think it ought to be the duty and ambition of all of us to improve the tone of parliament and keep it as high as possible.

That is just what I
was going to say. If there is any member of this House who does not want to be called a grafter, then do not let him graft. How does it come that the Department of Justice was able to accommodate the staff last year when the staff consisted of 22 officials? The minister says that they were somewhat cramped. This year there are still only 22 men and yet a great building outside of the department is to be provided at a .large expense besides retaining the old department. I cannot understand it. I think we are going too fast altogether. My Impression is that we ought to do with the departments that we have until we get the new buildings completed. I do not see the propriety of renting these buildings all over the city. I would not like to say that it was for the purpose of accommodating a friend. I do not want to impute that but we should have some explanation why the government are paying $6,500 rent, $2,000 taxes and $1,000 annually for the next five years for fitting up the building, making $9,500 a year to accommodate the customs officials when they were fully accommodated last year in the building that they now occupy for aught I know.
And the revenue falling off.

Yes, and the revenue falling off every day. There is something radically wrong and I think it is time we called a halt in these matters. But, I have not received a full explanation as to why the Justice Department require more room than they required last year to accommodate the same number of men. With regard to the statement that I was not a gentleman, I do not mind that at all.
I hope my hon. friend will not imagine that I suggested that he was not a gentleman.
I did not take it seriously.
I did not say it.
I have my own opinion and I set it up against that of the hon. gentleman.
Let me assure the hon. gentleman that I did not say he was not a gentleman.
You said that his conduct was not the conduct of a gentleman.
He asked me what I thought of his conduct and I said that I did not think it was consistent with the conduct of a gentleman to make that charge.
That is not what you said.

That is what I said. However, if I said anything that in any way suggested that the hon. gentleman was not a gentleman, I not only take it back but I apologize. No one could be in this House for six or eight months with the hon. gentleman as I have been, without recognizing that he is a gentleman in the highest sense of the word.
Perhaps I had better rise in my place now and say that the hon. Minister of Public Works is not a grafter.

Now, I want to give a little information, which I am sure will alter the opinion the hon. gentleman has formed as to the improvements of the government in giving this accommodation to the penitentiary branch. The customs house has been urging the necessity of larger premises. The Justice Department has been urging that larger accommodation should be provided for the penitentiary branch. We are transferring the customs house officials to the Seybold block so as to give them the requisite accommodation on two floors of the building. On the ground floor of the building which has been vacated we give accommodation to the penitentiary branch of the Justice Department. The total rent which we pay for the building which the penitentiary branch is to occupy is only $1,500. We give them the ground floor and we will have the upper floors still to be occupied by other departments.

I want to draw the attention of the minister to a statement he made a few minutes ago with reference to Mr. Caron. He said that he was only a carpenter working occasionally by the day. If he looks at page V-17 of the Auditor General's Report he will find that in nine months Mr. Caron worked 235 days at $2.50 a day, not a wet day or a day's lost time in the whole nine months.
I did not say he was working occasionally by the day; I said by the day and, being free to stay away if he pleased, if he did stay away he would be docked his day's pay.
He worked every day for nine months.
That shows that he is a very industrious man.
I understood the hon. gentleman to say that he was only a carpenter working occasionally by the day.

Who arranges as to what particular department shall occupy these various rented buildings? They are scattered all over the town.

This has been a matter of gradual expansion. The officers of a department urge the necessity for further accommodation, and then we ascertain where suitable premises can be got at the lowest possible rent. We consult the deputy heads of the different departments which desire the accommodation, and the final arrangements rest with the Public Works Department.

If it is absolutely necessary that all these buildings should be rented, which I very much doubt, it would be much better if some system were applied to the arrangement of offices. The present system leads to a great deal of inconvenience to the public, and I have no doubt to a great deal of inconvenience to the officials and to the departments. Even a person who lives in the city has great difficulty in finding where a certain branch of a department may be located so as to get the official you want. A stranger coming to the city must lose a great deal of time trying to discover where he is to go. Why should not the whole of one of these buildings be used for one particular department? Wrhy should the Interior Department, for instance, and the Department of Agriculture as well, he scattered all over the town in different buildings?

I admit it is extremely inconvenient, but it must be borne in mind that these buildings did not become available at the same time, and we have had to do the best we could. The heads of the different departments have tried to keep tlie branches together, and I think it is recognized that the Department of Public Works has endeavoured to do the best it could under the circumstances.
I understand some of these leases run for a good many years.
Some for ten years and some for five.
Is it the intention of the government to go on with the new building?
Yes.
What does the government intend to do writh these long leases when the building is finished?

It is not supposed that these new buildings, which are very extensive, will be finished very much before the expiry of these various leases. We have endeavoured to fix the term so that we will be able to occupy them until the new buildings are completed.
