We have twice within the last few years arranged our business with the city of Ottawa, giving the city a liberal consideration in view of the fact that these buildings pay no taxes. In consideration of fire protection and water and the non-payment of taxes, we paid originally $00,000 a year, and I think that finally we raised the amount to $100,000"a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We did not increase the amount; it is still $60,000, but we increased the period.
Then you paved Wellington street.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was under the old agreement.

You did some other things as well. Under that arrangement you gave the city of Ottawa a pretty liberal consideration. Now, the fact that you rent all these buildings and then turn round and pay taxes on them, means that the government are losing so much money which they would not lose if they had their own buildings, because these would not be taxable. The hon. minister asks why we

should occupy these rented buildings and pay no taxes on them, X might remind him that if he went into any town of Ontario and agreed to employ in any industry as many labouring people as are employed in these buildings, and paid the same amount of wages that are being paid to these people, it would not hesitate a moment to pay a bonus of $10,000 and exemption from taxation for ten years or perhaps twenty years.

But this industry is located here permanently and cannot be taken away.
Mr. SI'ROUIjE. The very fact that we are continuing here an industry which is growing rapidly is a reason why we should be dealt with more liberally by the city of Ottawa, and not be compelled to pay taxes on every building we occupy. Of course, the city might say : ' Well, get your own buildings.' I frankly think that it would be better for the country if we got our own buildings. I think it would cost us less than it does to-day. X am not very well informed with regard to the rents in Ottawa, but I would consider the rents we are paying for some of these buildings very high for most parts of this country. I do not know how they are struck.
They are based usually on the number of superficial feet occupied.

The parties who succeed in getting these buildings rented to the government as a rule get rich very fast, so that I take it that they are renting at a pretty liberal figure. This year we have added three more buildings, aggregating a rental of $32,500. Surely there is not such an addition to the staff of this government as to require that much additional space every year.
If you will go round, you will find every one of them occupied.

I am told that the employees are so thick in these buildings that they are almost tumbling over each other, and I presume that accounts for the additional buildings. The large number of employees we have in this city would make a city' anywhere, and it seems to me that the city of Ottawa ought to deal a little more liberally with the government than it is doing at the present time. But the government should make a more energetic move to get the necessary land and erect suitable buildings of our own.

We have all the land now. Some has been bought by agreement and the rest expropriated. The moment the Crown files its plan in the registry office the title is vested in the Crown, and then it is simply a question of valuation. Anxious as we all are to have these public buildings erected as speedily as possible, if I had
asked the Minister of Finance to put $1,000.000 in the estimates last fall, in the financial condition that existed, would he have done so, or would the House have approved of his doing so? We think we have pursued a prudent course in going slowly this year. With regard to the taxes, it must be borne in mind that these parliament buildings are a fixture in this city and that there are no taxes on them. They get fire and police protection and the benefit of water.
All of which we are paying for.

An agreement was made some years ago between the government and the city, by which the government agreed to do certain works and make certain improvements on Wellington street and in connection with two bridges and in connection with Major Hill Park and some other matters, in consideration of which the city agreed not to impose a tax on the salaries of civil servants derived from the government. So far as these other buildings are concerned, they were required for the use of the government. The owners of these buildings were at the time paying taxes to the city. Suppose the Public Works Department had sent one of its officials to say to the city : We are crowded for room and we must rent buildings, but we want you to waive taxes on these buildings in consideration of our renting them. The city council would answer -. We have nothing to do with your renting or not renting the buildings. So long as they are occupied by private owners they pay taxes to the city, and if you rent them we shall still expect to be paid taxes by the owners of the buildings. I could not make any answer to that.
Is the minister aware that the government had the Seybold building rented before?
Yes.
At what rental?
The same.
You did not pay taxes?

I do not know about the taxes. We offered Mr. Seybold $6,500 and the matter was under negotiation for some four months. We refused to pay the rental he asked and he was of the opinion that the department treated him rather harshly in refusing to pay a higher rental. We are paying a reasonable rental, not more than private individuals would be obliged to pay for the same accommodation.

I have been impressed with the fact that, if we are to judge from the increased superficial area of floor space used by the departments in Ottawa, the civil service must have more than doubled

in the last ten years. The population of Canada has not doubled in that time, and I do not see the necessity for such an increase.
The business of the country has more than doubled.

The trade has, but it does not follow that because the trade has increased the number of employees must increase in the same ratio. With proper organization, if ten men can do $100,000 worth of trade, 20 men can do three times that amount. There is a strong opinion in the country that a good organizer could so arrange the work and organize the staff so that the work that is done to-day could be done with one-half the present staff.
Has my hon. friend ever tried to correct that erroneous impression in the country?

If I was put on my oath I would swear to it. I think it is high time that either the Civil Service Commission or some other intelligent body should reorganize the service and show results by work and not increase the staff as it has been increased. At the present rate we would have before long all the buildings in Ottawa used by the departments and there has been no such growth in the population of Canada.
A second Canada has grown up in the last ten years.

Yes, a second Canada has grown up very different from the Canada that preceded it; it is a Canada not creditable to her history in respect of extravagance or administration. I believe we are approaching a stage when there will be a new Canada to take its place.
What steps does the minister take to arrive at a fair rental for buildings in this city?

The officers of the department make very careful inquiry, look into the assessment value, consider what would be a fair rental on the value of the property, inquire as to the prices at which buildings similarly situated are rented to private individuals, banks, &c., and see at what rate other buildings can be secured, and so endeavour to arrive at a fair valuation. I think my hon. friend, on inquiry, will agree that the rental we pay for the Canadian building of 41 cents per superficial foot is very reasonable.
Would the minister give the total rent paid and the amount of taxes paid by the government for one of these buildings; so that we may form some estimate as to its fairness?

Let us take the Canadian building. The total rental we pay is $42,539.60, and we pay $3,311 taxes.
Mr. SPROULE

If the taxes are $3,311. that would mean that the assessed value of the property is about $165,000, for the taxes in the city run about two per cent on the assessed value. If the government is paying $42,539 rent, that means that the minister is paying about twenty-five per cent of the assessment every year for the use of the buildings.

Does the hon. gentleman know anything about the building ? It is a very expensive building. I am satisfied that $165,000 would not begin to represent the value of the land and building. It is a structure of eight stories, very large, exceedingly well constructed and fitted up in modem style.

I have nothing to say against the Canadian building ; it is an exceedingly good building.
Mr, PUGSLEY. Will my hon. friend say. from his knowledge of the value of real estate in the city, that such a building, located as this is in a business centre, is too highly paid for at a rental of forty-one cents per superficial foot ?
I am not in the business, and do not know whether that rental is high or low, but does the minister think it right to pay twenty-five per cent of the assessed value ?
I do not know that that is the assessed value.

But the hon. minister has said that the taxes are $3,311, which would indicate an assessment of $165,000. I do not know whether the forty-one cents per superficial foot is a fair rent or not. I know that the building is an exceedingly good one
From the inquiries I have made from people who are qualified to speak, I am led to believe that a rental of forty-one cents per foot is a very reasonable rental.
I do not know about that but surely the minister will not say that it is reasonable to pay twenty-five per cent on the assessed value

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But is it safe to assume that the assessed value is the real value ?
In some cases it would and in some cases it would not. But there are no places in Ottawa, or any other city that I know of that should be rented at twenty-five ner cent of their assessed value.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman should not dwell so much on the assessed value. All over the country property is under valued for assessment purposes. I venture to say that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Perley>
would not sell his own house at its assessed value.

The argument of the hon. minister (Mr. Fielding) is fair in a way. But the assessed value in Ottawa is supposed to be the real value, although it may not be so in all cases. But, even allowing a large margin, the minister will hardly claim that it is fair to pay a rental representing such a high rate on the assessment.
Yukon public building-rent, repairs, fuel, light, water services and caretakers' salaries. &c., $100,000.
That item may be reduced to $85,000. One quarter of this and all votes have already been granted. On that basis, if $60,000 is voted now, that would give the amount needed.
What is the nature of these expenditures ?
They are for government huose, post office, and the administration building. Then there is the court house. Then departmental stores at Dawson, post office at Whitehorse.
What do we want with departmental stores?
I presume this place is required for stores of the different departments. These would be telegraph stores, we have a telegraph department there.
This seems to be a very large amount, $85,000 for taking care of public buildings in the Yukon.

That includes salaries of the agent, the clerk of works and the accountant. The clerk of works gets $3,000. He is a master builder. Mr. Bertram is the superintendent. Wages are very high in the Yukon.
Rideau Hall, including grounds-improvements, furniture and maintenance, $35,000.

This amount is required for maintenance of the buildings and grounds, the details of which I have here, and will read if desired. The total spent last year was $33,393.63. It was about an average year, and the items of about 'the same character.
Mr.' FOWLER. Under whose superintendence is this money expended?
There is a clerk of works who looks after all this expenditure, Mr. Hutchison. He reports to, and confers with, the chief architect.
I understood one of these items was $3,000 for crockery.
Furniture and crockery.
There must have been a good deal of waste in crockery. How much a year for carpets?
Carpets, linen and dry goods, $2,996.

We have the most disgraceful ramshackle building down there that can be imagined. To pay $35,000 a year on it, exclusively of another charge of $8,000 for fuel on this disgraceful old building-I cannot understand where the money is spent on it. I-think if that building were taken away and a' decent building erected in modem style, it could be maintained for considerably less than the amount it costs us to-day. People who come here from abroad and go down to see the residence of the Governor General are not impressed with the greatness of Canada, and wonder how we allow the figurehead of this great nation to live in such an old barn of a building. The Minister of Public Works should see that a decent public building is erected there that could be maintained at a reasonable expense.

There is a great deal of course in what my hon. friend says. The building is not at all attractive on the outside, it is not impressive, it is everything else but impressive. As my hon. friend says, it is not calculated to convey to visitors a fair idea of the greatness and wealth of Canada. Last session of parliament there was an appropriation of $100,000 voted for improvements. The idea was to make a facade in front of the building, to take away the present front and make a considerable improvement. Tenders were called for, and they were received shortly after I became minister. The lowest tender, if I remember rightly, was $275,000. I felt that I was not justified in entering into a contract for two reasons. One was that I did not think I would bejustified in expending so large an amount of money upon Rideau Hall. I thought the feeling of the country would be that it would be better to erect a new government house rather than expend that sum on repairs. Another reason was that, parliament having voted only $100,000, the members would feel that they ought to cover the total expenditure. Indeed, when the Acting Minister of Public Works asked for that vote he thought it would cover the cost. Therefore I declined to accept any of the tenders, and returned the cheques. So nothing has been done. I wish myself that it were possible to erect a government house which would be worthy of Canada and worthy of the empire to which we belong. I do not myself approve of the site of government house. I think a little further down the river, in the vicinity of Roekliffe, would be a much preferable site. Overlooking the Ottawa river there is a site which, for grandeur and magnificence, I do not believe could be surpassed or equalled anywhere in the world, and if it were possible to acquire a site there and to erect a suitable government house I believe the people of Canada would approve of the necessary expenditure. However, now is not the



time, for reasons hon. gentlemen can well understand, to engage in that expenditure. It is better to get along for a little while with the building that we have, even although it is not creditable. I would very much prefer myself considering the idea of erecting a new and suitable building upon a proper site-such a site as can be obtained-rather than spend a large amount of money in repairing or Improving the present building.

I think the minister did wisely in refusing to entertain the idea of spending very much money upon the repair of an old building like that. It is never a good plan to repair an old building anyway. I do not know the site to which the hon. gentleman refers, but, in my opinion, the people of Canada would be perfectly satisfied to spend a reasonable amount of money, and it seems to me that the money spent for repairs on this old building would be sufficient in itself to erect a new building.
Would the minister tell us what was spent on capital account on Rideau Hall last year ?
If my hon. friend will look at the Debates he will see the answer I gave to that question.
I suppose if I look up the Auditor General's Report, the report of the department and the Debates I might get the information and I would not have to ask this question.
I am very sorry I Ijfave not the memorandum here with respect to it.
The hon. gentleman should have the documents here.

I have not the papers with me showing that expenditure, the vote having been passed some time ago, and it would be utterly impossible for me to carry in my head all the items of expenditure throughout the country.
Will the minister bring down the information ?

I will be very glad to get it for my hon. friend.
Furniture-Dominion public buildings, $12,-
000.
Mr. PUGSLEY'. This is for public buildings all over the Dominion. Last year the total expenditure was $11,258.40. We are asking for $12,000.
Post Office-fittings and supplies, $30,000.

I would move that the item be changed to ' Dominion public buildings-fittings and supplies ' as it applies to other buildings as well. It is intended to apply part of this vote to the purchasing of Mr. PUGSLEY.
bag racks for use in various post offices. I think it is what they call the Harrison Bag Rack.
Is that a new patent ?
No.

Amendment agreed to.
Dominion cattle quarantine stations-renewals, repairs, &c., $20,000.

This is the same vote as last year. It is for the construction of corrals and dipping vats all along the boundary line between Canada and the United States and the maintenance of cattle quarantine stations throught the Dominion. This is in compliance with the request of the Department of Agriculture. Last year we expended $7,700.42.
You want $20,000 now.
The expenditure was low last year. This has been the usual vote for this purpose. There remained on the 1st January an unexpended balance of $13,000 which has lapsed.
Has the minister a record of the quantity of stock that is coming across the boundary line ?
I regret I have not. That will be in the Department of Agriculture. All I do is to provide the money.
I doubt very much if there is any stock at all coming across or any dipping to be done.
I think we should let that item stand until we get more information from the Minister of Agriculture.

I am quite wiling.
Item allowed to stand.
Dominion immigration buildings-repairs, furniture, &c., $4,500.

This is for making necessary repairs and renewals to all immigration buildings throughout the Dominion. Last year the expenditure was $4,701.55.
Dominion quarantine	stations-maintenance, &c., $4,000.
This is to make the necessary repairs to the different quarantine stations to keep them in proper state of efficiency.	.
What repairs have to be done at quarantine stations in the west, if it applies to the western country ?

I will give a statement showing how this money was distributed last year. There were repairs at Halifax, Sydney, Pictou, Charlottetown, Chatham. St John, Point Edward and Williams Head, B. C., the total expenditure being $8,565.68.

Ottawa public buildings-heating, including salaries of engineers, firemen and watchmen, $102,000.
Might I suggest to the hon. gentleman that he would add something to this vote to get a cooling apparatus in this chamber. The thermometer is now registering over 80 degrees.

I am inclined to think we might devise a plan to have the air passed through refrigerating compartments so that it would be fairly cool when it reaches the chamber. It would cost some money, but it is worth considering.
That was to have been done two years ago, when $25,000 was spent.
Not for that purpose.

If the Minister of Public Works would visit some of the better clubs and public buildings in London he would find that the temperature is kept at a proper mean during the year, and at very little expense. It is a shame to ask men to remain in this chamber in such heat as we have had to-day. I cannot believe that the officials who look after the ventilation of this building are doing their duty, and I trust the minister will investigate.

I think the only workable plan is to have the air pass through chamber cooled by the ammonia system.
I will ask my deputy and chief architect to see If some improvement cannot be made.

I am president of a company which uses a system of cold storage, and we produce a great many tons of ice per day at very little expense. I think a somewhat similar plant might be introduced in this House.
I will look into the matter.

I would suggest that the minister should consult Mr. D. B. Gosselin, a gentleman who was born in his own county, but who is now a resident of the United States, and who has been most successful in the cooling of factories and large public buildings. Mr. Gosselin has installed a system of cooling and cleansing the air in my factory which has proven most satisfactory. In some departments of my factory it is absolutely essential to have the air cool and dry, and since Mr. Gosselin introduced this system we can work at four degrees higher temperature than formerly. I think the minister should consult him about the ventilation of this chamber.
If my hon. friend gives me his address, I shall ask the chief architect to get into communication with him.
I shall do so.

I am afraid the only perfect remedy is to have shorter sessions.
349i

That would not remedy the trouble, because the air in the winter time in this chamber is generally vitiated.
I find it exceedingly difficult to sit in the House for long even in the winter months, because the temperature is kept unnecessarily high, and as a rule the air is foul. I would suggest that the vote be reduced so that we might buy less coal to burn and then there would not be so much heat. A great many of the members have been rendered ill from sitting in this hot and foul atmosphere.
I will think of that, too.
Could not something be done in the way of opening the windows ?
If you open the windows you, would get a temporary current of air and prevent circulation. The chief architect will try it on Monday to show the result.

Another trouble is that we do not have sufficient sunlight in this chamber. The only place the sun ever did strike was on one of those windows and some clever person put green shades on to keep it out.

This is a most serious question, and there is no reason why a remedv should not be applied. The Minister of Public Works knows that in the theaters in London and in the large auditoriums which are sometimes situated in the centre of a building, where there is no outside ventilation, the air is always kept fresh and the temperature comfortable. There is no reason in the world why the health of the members of this House should be endangered because of lack of fresh air.

In any first-class public school you will find a goad system of ventilation that could be very well adopted here. There are the two processes ; you can either force the fresh air in and then force the foul air out, or you can exhaust the air in connection with the pressure in. The air in this chamber should be cooled, and this can only be done by the use of ice or by the adoption of some of the other cooling processes now used. There would be no trouble whatever in regulating the temperature of the air of this chamber to any point required. All that is necessary is a man with a head. If the architect's department have not heads, there are any number of men in the country who could fix this thing up. In winter time the air is often unbearable because the fans are not kept going. At the present time, the windows are open in the corridor, there is not the slightest motion of the air. The fresh air should be forced in by pressure and the foul air forced out of these doors. Either the men who are supposed to operate the fans

do not understand them or the fans are not properly placed.

I have a great deal of confidence In the chief architect, and he tells me that the system of ventilation here Is by forcing the cold air in from the top all along these galleries by means of pumps and drawing it off at the bottom of the chamber. I think it is remarkable that in this chamber, with over 20 members, the air is as pure as it is. What we want is in some way to cool the air, and I will have the chief architect look into the systems iu other places and see if we cannot improve the atmosphere in that respect.
Does the man who keeps the fans going keep them going at night ?
Yes, all the time the House is sitting.
When I came in the other morning, I asked one of the men why the fans were not going, and he said he had forgotton to turn them on at eleven o'clock in the morning.
As soon as we go out of the chamber at six o'clock the fans stop.
If so, that is contrary to orders.	'

When the minister is looking into the question of ventilation, I hope he will look into the ventilation of the halls and other rooms of this building. The moment one comes into the main hall from the fresh air, he finds himself in foul air.
How much of this item is required for the purchase of coal ?

Last year we purchased 6.000 tons of furnace coal at $0.90 a ton, 50 tons of bituminous slack at $4.75 and 300 tons of cannel coal at $8.60. This vote is also for engineers, assistant engineers, firemen, caretakers, &e.
What methods does the minister adopt in calling for tenders for coal ?

Advertisement in the Ottawa papers.
Ottawa public buildings-elevator attendants, $15,000.
What do you pay them ?

From $50 to $60 a month.
Ottawa public buildings-gas and electric light, including roads and bridges, $35,000.
What is the total amount paid for electric light ?
W ARMSTRONG. Has the minister considered running a plant for lighting purposes?
I am told there formerly was a system, but the present rate of $2 per annum for each light of 16 candle power is regarded as much more economical. There are 11,382 lights.
What is meant by roads and bridges in this vote?

We light the Laurier bridge and the roads to the Experimental Farm and Rideau Hall.
Telephone service, $9,850.
Mr. PUGSLEY". There is an increase of $1,000. The telephone service is increasing; it seems to be regarded as one of the necessaries of life.
Do you supply telephones in the homes of civil servants?

No, only in the homes of the chief officers of the departments. For instance in the Customs Department, they are supplied at the residence of the private secretary, the assistant commissioner and the accountant.
What about the Public Works Department?
In connection with the Public Works Department there are 51 telephones altogether.
What price is paid?

We pay a flat rate for office and residence of $35. There are additional charges for desk and wall extension sets. The city rate is $45 for a wall set in an office and $25 for a wall set in a private residence. We get the benefit of a fiat rate of $35 on business phones, and of course the great majority of ours are business phones.
Grounds, Ottawa public buildings, $7,500.
This is a vote to pay for the care of the grounds in connection with the public buildings and also the walk which extends around the grounds.
Do the government own the ground in front of the building?
Of course the government does.
One would not think so.
Why not ?

A stranger approaching here in the afternoon would imagine that he was on the shores of New Brunswick, or Nova Scotia, in some such constituency as that represented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) where the fishing industry is extensively carried on and that the fishermen were drying their nets. It does not strike me as being proper that the very grounds in front of this building should be given over as a playground for any people,

I care not whether they are members of parliament, civil servants or the general public of the city. I think the grounds immediately in front of this House might be reserved, not as a playground, but as a beauty spot as my hon. friend suggested. I do not think it is at all impressive for strangers to come here to this parliament House and see these grounds devoted to the purpose for which they are now used. The reason why I ask in whom the ownership is was in consequence of a letter X received -and I suppose other members of parliament received the same :
Dear Sir,-You are most heartily invited to use at any time and to any extent the tennis courts, bowling green, quoit beds or cricket lawn of the Civil Service Amateur Athletic Association on Parliament Hill.
I supposed that these belonged to the Civil Service Amateur Athletic Association. It looked like an act of great kindness, of condescension, on the part of the association to extend to me this kindly invitation. I may use their cricket lawn-I suppose that is part of the ground in front of this building. I may use their tennis court, their quoit beds, their bowling green. I suppose I am to supply my own materials for the game, and then X am permitted, graciously permitted-I and other members of parliament to whom this most generous invitation is extended-to use the grounds. That is, I suppose, when they are not occupied. That would go without saying, that it was not in occupation by the people who own it. Now, I do not think, under the circumstances, in view of the fact that I have received this invitation, in view of the fact, as the invitation expressly states that the grounds are the property of the Civil Service Amateur Athletic Association, that my question should cause surprise. I would like to know from the minister how the grounds were transferred to this association, whether by deed of gift in the ordinary way, by His Majesty, the King, or if in the previous reign, by Her Majesty, the Queen, or whether by formal Act of parliament ? In what way did the government of this country divest itself of this property ? It would not be by expropriation-that would be the other way round. It seems to me the minister should not have expressed the view that I was not serious when I asked as to this ownership. He must see that I have very strong reasons for asking the question in the manner in which I did. For, certainly, when the Civil Service Amateur Athletic Association speak of their cricket lawn, tennis ground, bowling green and quoit beds, one would suppose they had in some way acquired an absolute ownership of this property. And this $7,000 vote, it seems, is devoted-a considerable portion of it at least-to keeping up these quoit beds, cricket grounds, tennis courts and bowling greens. It does seem to me this requires some explanation on the part of the minister. Do they actually own this property ? Or have they leased it ? Or have they acquired it by taking possession of it 7 The minister might point out how they have acquired it, and also say whether they are able to keep off the general populace. I have thought over this several times when, in passing, I have seen these people disporting themselves on the green, and have wondered how they came to acquire the title in the first place. Perhaps they took it by forcible possession. If they have no title, by what right do they keep off the general public ? If they say the grounds are public, that might give them a right from one standpoint. But would it give them the right to keep the public off ? Why should not the people of the city-the people who pay the taxes, for the civil servants do not pay taxes-come here and play baseball, or 'cricket, or any other game 1 Or exercise their horses, use the place as a riding ground ? Or teach the equestrian art to their children ? I fail to see why it should not be used by the general public. It appears, however, that the Civil Service have acquired an absolute title to the property. I would like to have an explanation from the hon. minister.
This is a legacy which has come down to me from my predecessor-

If the minister will pardon me, in the eight years I have been a member of this House, I have never seen these games carried on to the same extent as this year. I was not here under the old government, and do not know what was done at that time. But before the present minister came, I never saw anything like what goes on now.

I made inquiry with reference to the use of the grounds and found that, a considerable time ago, permission was given to the members of the civil service to use the green in front of the west block for a bowling green, and to use the grounds in front of the parliament buildings for tennis and other games. I may say very frankly that I had some doubts whether or not it would be better for me to issue notice discontinuing the use of the grounds in front of the parliament buildings. But as I have seen, within the-last few days, the boys and girls enjoying themselves on that beautiful lawn, I hesitated about depriving them of that pleasure. Perhaps I was a little too tenderhearted. However, I decided to let matters go on this year, at all events, as in recent years. But' if there is any general expression of feeling on the part of members of the House that this rule should be countermanded, and this permission rescinded, I shall be disposed to act upon it.
What does the minister thing of the circular ?

I think it should not be construed too critically. I presume they merely intended to say that if a fine looking gentleman like my hon. friend from Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler) would go down and have a game of tennis, there is the tennis net which he can use, there are the pretty girls, and he might have a delightful game of tennis. So with all the members of parliament. It was intended, I am sure, as a kindly invitation to the members to go there and join in tennis, join in baseball, join in bowling upon the green. I do not myself feel that the members of the Civil Service Association intended anything but to extend a courteous invitation to the members to join with them in their games on the parliament grounds. - The permission is only a temporary one. It was given by one of my predecessors, and can be countermanded at any time.

I think if the minister had acted according to his first thought he would have acted wisely and well. Because if the Civil Service Association have a right to use those grounds they have no greater right than the general public. If the hon. gentleman was influenced in permitting the thing to continue by reason of the fact that the boys and girls were disporting themselves there, that should influence him to extend the privilege so that more boys and girls might have the opportunity of enjoying themselves. Therefore it should not be confined to the civil service. I think as a matter of fact he should allow the civil servants to obtain a ground somewhere else, and reserve these grounds from use.
Major's Hill Park, $6,000.

That is for the purpose of keeping the park in proper condition. The sum includes salaries of the assistant superintendent, the guardian, and the pay of the men. It is intended to extend the park down towards Nepean Point, and beautify it.

We have been expending and beautifying that park for the last thirty years, and now that we have succeeded in making it attractive and ornamental, we turn around and allow the railway company to disfigure the whole thing.

We will discuss that later.
Some resolutions reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.
What business on Monday?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will take up the Bill respecting the lead bounties and Chinese immigration, and the Minister of Public Works will continue Supply. If there are other Bills non-contentious, we will take them up.

I wish again to call attention to a letter which I think was addressed to Mr. Shearer some time in April last, a copy of which I have asked to be brought down. No attention is paid to my request, and I have to repeat it again and again. Perhaps it is because I made the request to the First Minister. I would like to say so in his presence, because he has repeatedly treated requests of mine in the same way. I want to say that I will take an early opportunity of referring to it, if that is the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is not the slightest intention on the part of the Prime /Minister to be discourteous to my hon. friend. It has been overlooked in the multiplicity of things, and I will call his attention to it.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 11.15 p.m.
